sections.html:
The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building, 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. The full deed and index collection, 1805 to the present, is kept there on books and microfilm.

Older material sits at the County Records Center and Archives, 117 South Main Street, 6th floor, reached by the Main Street elevator. Call 937-225-6366 for the archives. Paperwork is recorded, scanned and indexed the day it arrives, whether it comes by mail, over the counter or from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department. Documents go back in the mail the next business day, and the office works from 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays.

The base charge for the first two pages is $34.00, made up of $17 for the recorder and $17 for the housing trust fund under section 317.32 of the Ohio Revised Code. Each added page is $8.00. A county may add a preservation surcharge of up to $5, which brings the first two pages to $39.00 where it applies. Call the office to confirm the total the day you file.

Montgomery County recording charges
ChargeAmount
First two pages$34.00, or $39.00 with the preservation surcharge
Each added page$8.00
Mortgage release or assignment, marginal notation$4.00
No clear 3-inch top margin on page one$20.00 standardization fee

Pay at the counter in cash, or by check or money order made out to Montgomery County Recorder.

The clerk at the window checks for these elements. A deed needs:

  • The names of the buyers and sellers.
  • A legal description, which you can get from the Copy Center.
  • The sellers' signatures.
  • A preparation statement, if the deed was notarized in Ohio.
  • A Transfer or No Transfer stamp from the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department, plus the Engineer's approval where the property calls for it.

Notarization follows the law of the state where the signer stood. The notary block has to show a statement, a signature and an expiration date. A mortgage adds the loan amount and the lender and borrower names.

Changing a name on a deed means a new deed, a stop at the Auditor for a stamp and then the Recorder. Paying off a loan creates no new deed. Instead the lender records a Release or Satisfaction of Mortgage.

sections.h2: Transfers that visit the Auditor first
sections.html:
Anything that conveys land passes through the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department before recording. Under section 319.202 the buyer files a value statement, and the grantor pays the fee set in section 319.54, plus any transfer tax the county commissioners have levied.

For e-recording, mortgages, assignments and releases with no transfer can go in electronically through Simplifile. Deeds and anything needing a No Transfer stamp, such as a transfer on death designation, an easement or an affidavit that references a deed, must be mailed or walked through the Auditor's department first.

The Auditor and Engineer also publish conveyance standards, adopted August 2, 2021, governing legal descriptions and splits. Copies are on the Auditor's third and fifth floors and the Engineer's eighth floor at 451 West Third Street.

sections.h2: Finding and printing a recorded deed
sections.html:
Print any document you find on the Recorder's online search at no charge. If you cannot print, the Copy Center charges $2.00 per page, and certification adds $1.00. Staff do not run title searches, but the 5th floor Public Research Area has public computers for doing your own.

  • Deeds, releases and liens are searchable by name on the county's online system.
  • A veteran who recorded a DD214 can request a copy at no charge, and the Recorder issues a free Veteran ID card to those who record one.

Searching by street address happens on the Auditor's site instead of the Recorder's.

sections.h2: Tracing the history of an older house
sections.html:
Start with the chain of ownership in the Recorder's deed records, using either the alphabetical grantee-grantor index or the tract index, which is organized by legal description. Both index types run from 1805 to the present, with deed books and microfilm for 1935 on and microfilm for 1805 through 1934. Build the chain of owners from there, then check the Auditor's tax lists for hints about when the house was built.

  • At the Records Center and Archives, the alphabetical indexes cover 1805 to the present, and tract index microfilm covers 1805 to 1934.
  • The Auditor's tax lists run 1803 to 1954 as indexes and 1955 to 1985 as original books.
  • A jump of more than 50% in one year's taxable value usually points to construction or improvements.

Taxable values have been recorded at 35% of market value since 1973, and at 40 to 45% before that. The research is the individual's job, though the archives answer questions at 937-225-6366. New records are indexed the day they arrive, which keeps the chain current for a title search.

sections.h2: What to bring when you file in person
sections.html:
Walking a deed through two offices goes smoothly when the packet is complete. Gather the signed and notarized deed, the buyer's value statement, the legal description and a way to pay both the auditor's conveyance fee and the recorder's charge. If the property needs the Engineer's approval, get that first.

Ask your title agent whether they will deliver the deed or whether you are expected to. When they handle it, the recorded deed comes back by mail the next business day after recording. When a mortgage is being paid off, the lender records its own release, so look the release up in the online search a few weeks after closing.

Dayton is the county seat, and the county has roughly 230,000 parcels. The county had 539,598 residents in 2025 and 254,375 housing units. Owners occupy 62.5% of homes, the median owner-occupied value is $180,900, and median gross rent is $1,026. Median household income is $66,139.

More than a third of homes are rented, so many sellers here are landlords. The Auditor's deed endorsement for residential rental property reminds the buyer to file landlord information under section 5323.02, so a rental sale carries one more form than an owner-occupied home.

Whether the buyer pays cash or finances, the path is the same: Auditor stamp first, then the Recorder. A cash sale simply leaves out the mortgage that a lender would otherwise record.

faqs.q: What is the address of the Montgomery County Recorder?
faqs.a: The Recorder's Office is on the 5th floor of the County Administration Building at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. Records Center and Archives material is at 117 South Main Street, 6th floor.

faqs.q: How much does Montgomery County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The state schedule is $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per added page, and a $5 preservation surcharge can bring two pages to $39.00. Call the office to confirm the figure the day you file.

faqs.q: Do I need the Auditor before the Recorder in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Yes, for any deed. The Auditor's Deed Transfer Department stamps it Transfer or No Transfer and collects the conveyance fee, then the deed goes to the Recorder. Only non-transfer papers such as mortgages and releases can be e-recorded directly.

faqs.q: Is there a fee for a poorly formatted document in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: Yes. A $20 standardization fee applies when page one lacks a clear 3-inch top margin, and all Ohio standardization laws apply.

faqs.q: Can I get a free copy of my Montgomery County deed?
faqs.a: Yes, if you print it yourself from the Recorder's online search. The Copy Center charges $2.00 per page if you cannot print, with certification costing $1.00 more.
